description: Six Hindu festivals — Holi to Raksha Bandhan — and Hindu ethics on the environment and social inclusion.
content_html:
Hindu Festivals: Marking the Sacred Year

Hindu festivals (utsav) celebrate the divine through colour, light, story, music and community. Most are tied to the lunar calendar and commemorate events from sacred narratives or honour specific deities. Festivals are understood as spiritually charged moments when the power of the divine is especially accessible, and participation generates spiritual merit. Six festivals are specifically required for study: Holi, Navaratri, Diwali, Maha Shivaratri, Ganesh Chaturthi and Raksha Bandhan.

Holi: The Festival of Colours

Holi is celebrated in late February or March to mark the arrival of spring and the victory of good over evil. Its central narrative concerns Prahlad, a devoted worshipper of Vishnu whose father, the demon king Hiranyakashipu, tried to have him killed because he refused to worship his father instead of God. Hiranyakashipu’s sister Holika, who was believed to be immune to fire, tricked Prahlad into sitting with her in a bonfire. However, Holika burned while Prahlad emerged unharmed through Vishnu’s protection. Bonfires are lit the night before the main celebrations (Holika Dahan), symbolising the burning of evil. The following day, people celebrate joyfully by throwing powdered colours and water at each other, symbolising the arrival of spring and the joy of divine protection.

Holi is also associated with the playful love (lila) of Krishna and Radha. The festival temporarily dissolves normal social boundaries — differences of caste, age and gender are suspended as people play together. This social dimension gives Holi significance beyond its mythological roots, representing the Hindu ideal of joyful community and equality before God.

Navaratri: Nine Nights of the Goddess

Navaratri means “nine nights” and is celebrated twice a year, with the most significant occurrence in autumn (Sharad Navaratri). It honours the goddess Durga and her nine forms (the Navadurga), celebrating the divine feminine power known as Shakti. The festival commemorates the goddess’s victory over the buffalo demon Mahishasura, as narrated in the Devi Mahatmya. Each of the nine nights honours a different form of the goddess. In Gujarat, celebrants perform the lively group dances garba and dandiya raas. In West Bengal, the last four days are called Durga Puja, ending with the immersion of large clay images of Durga in rivers. On the tenth day (Vijaya Dashami or Dussehra), large effigies of the demon Ravana are burned, linking Navaratri to the story of Rama’s victory over Ravana in the Ramayana.

Diwali: The Festival of Lights

Diwali, the festival of lights, typically falls in October or November. It celebrates the return of Rama and Sita to Ayodhya after Rama’s fourteen-year exile and his defeat of the demon king Ravana, as narrated in the Ramayana. The citizens of Ayodhya lit rows of clay lamps (diyas) to welcome them home — this is re-enacted today as millions of diyas, candles and electric lights illuminate homes and public spaces. Diwali is also the time to worship the goddess Lakshmi (goddess of wealth and prosperity), and new account books are begun by Hindu businesses at Diwali. Fireworks are set off as expressions of joy and to drive away evil.

Diwali lasts five days, each with its own rituals, including the exchange of sweets and gifts. For Vaishnava Hindus, it primarily honours Rama’s return; for many other Hindus, it is primarily Lakshmi’s festival. It is widely shared beyond Hinduism — Jains celebrate Diwali as the anniversary of Mahavira’s moksha, and Sikhs celebrate the release of Guru Hargobind from captivity.

Key Fact

The story behind Diwali comes from the Ramayana: Rama (an avatar of Vishnu) defeats the demon Ravana and returns home to Ayodhya after fourteen years. The lamps lit at Diwali represent the triumph of light over darkness, knowledge over ignorance, and good over evil — all core Hindu values.

Maha Shivaratri, Ganesh Chaturthi and Raksha Bandhan

Maha Shivaratri (“the great night of Shiva”) falls in late winter and is one of the most important occasions for Shaivite Hindus (devotees of Shiva). Worshippers fast all day and keep an all-night vigil, chanting Shiva’s names and meditating. Shiva lingam shrines in temples are bathed with water, milk and honey and decorated with bael leaves. The festival commemorates the night when Shiva performed the cosmic dance (Tandava) that sustains the universe, and is also associated with the night of Shiva and Parvati’s divine wedding.

Ganesh Chaturthi celebrates the birthday of Ganesh, the elephant-headed son of Shiva and Parvati. It is especially prominent in Maharashtra, where large clay images of Ganesh are installed in homes and public pandals for ten days of worship, music and celebration. On the final day (Anant Chaturdashi), the images are carried in large processions to rivers or the sea and immersed, symbolising Ganesh’s return to his cosmic home. Ganesh is worshipped at the beginning of any new enterprise because he is the remover of obstacles (Vighnaharta) and the patron of beginnings. The 19th-century social reformer Bal Gangadhar Tilak transformed Ganesh Chaturthi into a large public festival as a means of bringing Hindus together during the colonial period.

Raksha Bandhan (“the bond of protection”) is a festival honouring the relationship between brothers and sisters. Sisters tie a sacred thread (rakhi) around their brother’s wrist; the brother gives a gift and pledges to protect his sister. The festival has its roots in several Hindu narratives, including the goddess Lakshmi tying a protective thread on Bali, and is celebrated across India in late summer. It affirms family bonds and the principle of mutual care and duty (svadharma).

Hindu Ethics: The Environment and Ahimsa

Hindu attitudes to the environment are rooted in the belief that Brahman pervades all of creation. Harming the natural world is therefore not merely a practical concern but a spiritual one. The Hindu concept of ahimsa (non-violence) applies not only to human beings but to animals and the natural world. The cow is particularly revered and protected. Sacred rivers like the Ganges are worshipped as goddesses, giving their protection spiritual as well as environmental weight.

In 1986, Hindu representatives participated in the Assisi Declarations on Nature, committing Hinduism formally to environmental stewardship grounded in its religious teachings. These declarations affirmed that nature is sacred, not merely useful, and that believers have a duty to protect it. In practical terms, Hindu organisations run goshallas (cow sanctuaries) across India. The Ahimsa Foundation for Cattle Protection works to end the slaughter of cows and to promote non-violent attitudes to animals.

Key Fact

The Hindu virtues most relevant to environmental ethics are: daya (compassion towards all living beings), dama (self-restraint, including restraint in consuming natural resources) and kshama (patience and tolerance). The Mahabharata teaches that one who harms no creature in thought, word or deed attains moksha. Mahatma Gandhi’s lifelong commitment to ahimsa and simple living embodied these values on a public scale.

Social Inclusion and Women’s Rights

Hindu teachings on social ethics are complex and contested. The Bhagavad Gita and other scriptures teach that all souls are equally sacred regardless of birth — the Gita at XVI 1–3 lists virtues including fearlessness, compassion and generosity as the marks of a divine character without reference to gender or caste. However, historical Hindu social structures have often restricted women’s roles and entrenched inequalities. Modern Hindu reformers including Gandhi and figures within the Swaminarayan and Brahma Kumaris traditions have emphasised the spiritual equality of women and have worked to expand women’s participation in leadership and religious practice.

Sewa International (also known as Sewa UK) is a Hindu charity providing disaster relief, food distribution, community care and education both in the United Kingdom and internationally. Its work is explicitly grounded in the Hindu principle of sewa (selfless service) as an expression of karma yoga. Projects range from flood relief in India to food banks in British cities. The work of the Purusha Sukta (Rig Veda) has been used to argue that all parts of society — all varnas — form one body, meaning that social inequality harms the whole community.

Hinduism presents divergent voices on women’s roles. Conservative interpretations of manusmriti (the Laws of Manu, a legal text, not part of the core Vedic or Gita canon) have historically been used to restrict women. However, many Hindus reject this as a distorted social text that misrepresents the Vedic and Gita vision. The Bhagavad Gita itself contains no restrictions based on gender. The goddess traditions (Shaktism, Vaishnavism through Radha, Shaivism through Parvati) present the divine feminine as supremely powerful. Modern Hindu movements increasingly emphasise that women and men are spiritually equal before Brahman, and that social barriers reflect cultural accretion rather than authentic Hindu teaching.

Mahatma Gandhi stands as the most globally recognised example of Hindu ethics applied to social and political life. Drawing on the Bhagavad Gita’s karma yoga (Bhagavad Gita II 47) and the principle of ahimsa, Gandhi developed satyagraha (“truth-force” or non-violent resistance) as a method of social and political change. He campaigned against the caste system, especially the treatment of those called “Untouchables” (whom he renamed Harijans, “children of God”), and promoted simple living as a form of environmental and social restraint (dama). Gandhi’s life demonstrated that Hindu ethics are not purely personal but can be powerful forces for social transformation.
exam_tip_html: For Outline and Describe questions about festivals, always include the story behind the festival and what the practices symbolise — examiners reward linking the practice to belief. For example, Diwali lamps represent the triumph of light over darkness; Holika Dahan represents the burning of evil through Vishnu’s protection. For the 15-mark Discuss on Hindu ethics (environment, social inclusion), name specific organisations and sources: the Assisi Declarations (1986), goshallas, Sewa International, the work of Gandhi, and the Bhagavad Gita. A common error is treating Hinduism as having a single view on social issues — always present divergent voices. Check spelling: ahimsa, Navaratri, Shivaratri, Ganesh Chaturthi, kshama and Sewa International are all assessed in SPaG on the extended response.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The six key Hindu festivals are Holi (colours and the victory of devotion), Navaratri (nine nights of the goddess Durga), Diwali (festival of lights, Rama’s return, Lakshmi worship), Maha Shivaratri (all-night vigil for Shiva), Ganesh Chaturthi (Ganesh’s birthday in Maharashtra) and Raksha Bandhan (the brother–sister bond).
  • Hindu environmental ethics are rooted in ahimsa (non-violence), the sacredness of the natural world, and the virtues of daya (compassion), dama (restraint) and kshama (patience). The 1986 Assisi Declarations formalised this commitment, and goshallas and Sewa International put it into practice.
  • Hindu teachings on social inclusion and women’s rights are contested: the Bhagavad Gita presents spiritual equality, but historical social structures have restricted women. Gandhi’s application of karma yoga and ahimsa to political life remains the most influential example of Hindu ethics in social action.

practice_questions.text: State the name of the Hindu festival that celebrates the victory of the devotee Prahlad over the demon Holika.
Describe what happens during the Hindu festival of Diwali.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Diwali, the festival of lights, involves lighting rows of clay lamps (diyas), candles and electric lights to illuminate homes and public spaces.
• It celebrates the return of Rama and Sita to Ayodhya after Rama’s defeat of Ravana, as narrated in the Ramayana.
• Hindus worship the goddess Lakshmi for wealth and prosperity, and exchange sweets and gifts.
• Fireworks are set off as expressions of joy and to drive away evil.
[1 mark for a basic description; 2 marks for a developed description that includes either the story/meaning or two distinct practices.]

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which Hindu beliefs lead to actions that protect the environment.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Hindu belief that Brahman pervades all creation means that harming nature is spiritually wrong, not merely a practical concern. This motivates conservation efforts.
• The principle of ahimsa (non-violence) extends to animals, inspiring the protection of cows through goshallas (cow sanctuaries) and organisations like the Ahimsa Foundation for Cattle Protection.
• Hindu reverence for sacred rivers such as the Ganges motivates campaigns to protect them from pollution.
• The 1986 Assisi Declarations on Nature committed Hindu leaders to environmental stewardship rooted in religious teaching.
• Sewa International carries out environmental and community projects in line with the karma yoga principle of selfless service.
[1 mark for one basic point; 2 marks for two basic points or one developed point; 3 marks for two points that both link Hindu belief to specific environmental action.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Ganesh Chaturthi reflects important Hindu beliefs about the divine.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Ganesh Chaturthi celebrates the birthday of Ganesh, the elephant-headed son of Shiva and Parvati. The ten days of worship with clay images reflect the belief that deities can be made present in sacred images (murti) for the duration of a festival and then returned to their cosmic home through immersion. This reflects the belief in darshan — that contact with the divine presence in a murti brings blessing.
• The immersion of the clay Ganesh image at the end of the festival reflects Hindu beliefs about the cyclical nature of divine presence: the deity is welcomed, worshipped and then ceremonially released back into the cosmic waters, reflecting the Hindu understanding of creation and dissolution as eternal cycles.
• The worship of Ganesh as the remover of obstacles (Vighnaharta) and patron of beginnings reflects the Hindu belief that deities have specific powers that can be invoked through devotion. Beginning any enterprise with Ganesh puja reflects the bhakti path — seeking divine help through devotion.
• The social dimension of Ganesh Chaturthi — originally promoted by Bal Gangadhar Tilak as a community festival — reflects the belief that religion binds communities together and that shared worship expresses social solidarity.
[6 marks: up to 3 marks per way — 1 for identifying the connection, 2 for developing the explanation, 3 for linking to a specific Hindu belief or concept.]

practice_questions.text: 'Hindu teachings about the environment are more important than Hindu teachings about social equality.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Hindu environmental ethics are deeply embedded in core beliefs: ahimsa (non-violence), the sacredness of creation and the principle that Brahman pervades all life make environmental care a fundamental spiritual duty.
• The 1986 Assisi Declarations on Nature gave formal religious authority to Hindu environmental commitment. Practical initiatives like goshallas and Sewa International show this being lived out on a large scale.
• The Mahabharata teaches that one who harms no creature attains moksha, giving environmental non-violence the highest possible spiritual weight.
• The river Ganges is worshipped as a goddess — environmental damage to her is literally an act of sacrilege, not merely a social problem.

Arguments against:
• Hindu teachings about social equality are arguably more urgently needed because human inequality causes immediate, preventable suffering. Gandhi saw challenging the caste system and ‘Untouchability’ as a core expression of karma yoga and ahimsa.
• The Bhagavad Gita’s teaching on spiritual equality — that all souls are equal before God regardless of birth — has radical implications for social justice. The Purusha Sukta presents society as one body, meaning social inequality harms the whole.
• The virtues of daya (compassion), dama (restraint) and kshama (patience) apply to human relationships as much as to the environment. A Hindu who practises daya must respond to human poverty and discrimination.
• Sewa International’s work spans both environmental projects and social welfare, suggesting that in practice Hindu ethics do not separate these concerns.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Bhagavad Gita XVI 1-3; Mahabharata; Assisi Declarations; Gandhi; goshallas; Sewa International); explicit weighing of the two forms of ethical concern; a justified conclusion.
Secure: Two sides with development; at least one named source per side; a conclusion that takes a position.
Developing: One side stronger; limited source use; partial conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided; no or incorrect sources; no real conclusion.
[15 marks; SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the meaning of Navaratri and its importance for Hindu worshippers.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Navaratri means ‘nine nights’; it honours the goddess Durga and her nine forms (Navadurga), celebrating the divine feminine power (Shakti).
• The festival commemorates Durga’s victory over the buffalo demon Mahishasura.
• In Gujarat, celebrants perform garba and dandiya raas dances; in Bengal, large clay Durga images are worshipped and then immersed.
• The tenth day (Vijaya Dashami/Dussehra) links Navaratri to the Ramayana through the burning of Ravana effigies.
• For worshippers, Navaratri affirms the power of the goddess and the importance of the divine feminine in Hindu life.
[1 mark for a basic outline; 2 marks for some development; 3 marks for a developed answer that includes the story, practice and significance.]

right: Festival of lights celebrating Rama's return and Lakshmi worship

flashcard_questions.q: What is the story behind the Hindu festival of Holi?
flashcard_questions.a: The devotee Prahlad survived a bonfire by Vishnu's grace; Holika burned instead. Holi celebrates devotion's triumph over evil.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Diwali celebrate and what is its main practice?
flashcard_questions.a: Rama's return to Ayodhya after defeating Ravana; rows of lamps (diyas) are lit to represent light's victory over darkness.

flashcard_questions.q: Which goddess is honoured during Navaratri?
flashcard_questions.a: Durga (and her nine forms, the Navadurga), celebrating Shakti — the divine feminine power.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens on the final day of Ganesh Chaturthi?
flashcard_questions.a: The clay Ganesh image is carried in procession and immersed in a river or the sea, symbolising Ganesh's return to his cosmic home.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the significance of Maha Shivaratri?
flashcard_questions.a: A night of fasting, all-night prayer and vigil honouring Shiva; associated with his cosmic dance and divine wedding to Parvati.
Sisters tie a rakhi (sacred thread) on their brother's wrist; the brother gives a gift and pledges protection.
Non-violence or harmlessness towards all living beings; one of the most fundamental Hindu moral principles.
Sanctuaries where cows are protected and cared for, expressing Hindu reverence for the cow as a sacred animal.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the 1986 Assisi Declarations on Nature commit Hinduism to?
flashcard_questions.a: Environmental stewardship and conservation, rooted in the Hindu belief that nature is sacred and Brahman pervades all creation.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three Hindu virtues most relevant to environmental and social ethics in this lesson.
How did Gandhi apply Hindu ethics to social and political life?
flashcard_questions.a: Through satyagraha (non-violent resistance), drawing on ahimsa and karma yoga (Bhagavad Gita II 47) to challenge injustice.
A Hindu charity providing disaster relief, education and community care; inspired by the principle of selfless service (sewa).

glossary_terms.definition: The Hindu festival of colours, celebrating the victory of devotion over evil through the story of Prahlad and Holika, and welcoming spring.
Nine nights of worship dedicated to the goddess Durga and her nine forms, celebrating divine feminine power (Shakti).
The festival of lights, associated with the return of Rama to Ayodhya, the worship of Lakshmi and the triumph of light over darkness.
The great night of Shiva; a night of fasting, prayer and all-night vigil honouring Shiva's cosmic dance and his wedding to Parvati.
The birthday festival of Ganesh; celebrated for ten days with clay images installed in homes and public spaces, then immersed in water.
A festival honouring the brother-sister bond; sisters tie a rakhi thread on their brother's wrist in exchange for a pledge of protection.
The active divine energy or power, especially the feminine principle of the divine; the energy that animates all existence.
Non-violence or harmlessness towards all living beings; one of the most fundamental moral principles in Hinduism.
Sanctuaries for cows where they are protected and cared for; an expression of Hindu reverence for the cow as a sacred animal.
A Hindu charity providing disaster relief, community care and education, rooted in the principle of selfless service (sewa) as karma yoga.
Compassion towards all living beings; a key Hindu virtue applying to both social ethics and environmental care.
Patience and tolerance; a Hindu virtue encouraging restraint of anger and openness to others.
